input.title: The Impossible Order
input.openingPromise: It is your first night shift alone in the Harbor Packing House. Order slips slide in on a rattling brass conveyor, each stamped with a fish count and packing rules. Real packers ship what can be packed — and refuse what cannot. Your stamp, your stock, your call. The harbor log remembers everything.
input.firstThreeSeconds: The screen opens already inside the packing house: rain streaks the window, a lantern swings, and the conveyor is ALREADY moving — a paper order slip slides in with a soft mechanical clack and unrolls itself center-screen: "PACK 12 FISH — EXACTLY 3 FISH PER ROW." Below it, a wooden grid crate waits, a glinting pile of silver fish sits in the stock bin at the left, and a fish is gently pulsing, begging to be dragged. Two big stamps sit at the bottom: green SHIP IT, red CANNOT BE PACKED. No menu, no instructions screen — the shift has begun.
input.firstAction: Drag one fish from the stock bin into the crate grid. It snaps into the top-left cell with a wet slap sound and the row outline lights up showing "1 of 3 in this row." Two more drags complete the row and it locks with a satisfying wooden CLUNK, the row turning ice-blue. The child immediately understands the whole physical grammar of the game — fish fill rows, complete rows lock, and the crate is being built toward the order — before a single word of tutorial is spoken.
input.coreInteraction: The child reads each order (a product plus one or two simultaneous structural constraints), then physically builds a rectangular array by dragging fish from a finite shared stock into a crate grid. The grid enforces mathematical structure: only complete equal rows lock (locked rows glow ice-blue); a partial or uneven row glows red, wobbles, and will not lock, and the SHIP IT stamp stays dim while any red exists. A live counter shows fish placed vs. fish ordered, and constraint badges on the order slip flip from grey to gold as each rule is currently satisfied — so the child can SEE that "rows of 3 ✓" is met while "more than 4 rows ✗" is not, forcing them to hold both constraints at once. When the child believes the arrangement meets the order, they slam SHIP IT. When they conclude no arrangement can exist, they slam CANNOT BE PACKED and must pick one justification from three short reasons ("nothing divides it evenly," "the rows don't come out even," "the rule breaks the count"); picking the right reason is part of being correct. Fish return to stock instantly on drag-out, so restructuring an attempt (tearing down 3×6 to try 6×3 or 2×9) is fast and frictionless — near-miss exploration is cheap, but shipping or refusing is a committed, stock-changing act.
input.mathAsPower: Multiplication IS the machine. The crate grid is a physical factor-pair engine: rows × fish-per-row must equal the ordered product, and the crate literally will not close otherwise. Every mathematical fact has a visible mechanical consequence — 17 fish in rows of more than one leaves a red, wobbling, unlockable stub row no matter how the child rearranges, making primality something you can feel with your hands; 25 in exactly 4 rows always strands one fish flashing red because 4 does not divide 25. Solving a missing factor (order says "rows of 6" for 24 fish) is answered by BUILDING the four rows, not by typing a number. Constraint synthesis is spatial: "more than 4 rows AND more than 4 per row" for 24 kills 6×4 and 4×6 visibly — gold badges refuse to both light — so the child must reason there is no factor pair of 24 with both factors above 4, and stamp the refusal. Stock arithmetic runs underneath: wrong shipments and refused-fillable orders drain a real counted supply, so multiplication and subtraction together decide whether the late-shift big order can even be attempted. Math changes the world; the world never accepts non-math.
input.stakes: The night's fish stock is finite and shared across every order (starting stock: 60 fish, shown as a real drawn pile that visibly shrinks). Ship a WRONG order and the inspection crane hoists the crate, the bottom drops, and every fish in it splashes into the black harbor water — gone from the shift forever. Refuse a FILLABLE order and the captain snorts, snatches their promised crate of bonus stock, and stomps off the dock — stock you will never receive. Late in the shift, the Festival Team Challenge order arrives: a big order that can only be filled if the child protected their stock with correct decisions earlier. Every stamp is therefore a bet placed with real, countable resources the child can see dwindling.
input.consequences: Wrong SHIP: the crane-dunk animation plays (2.5s, dramatic but not mocking), the exact spilled count floats up in red ("−15 fish"), and the stock pile visibly shrinks; the order slip returns stamped "REJECTED BY INSPECTOR — count the rows" so the child sees WHY (e.g., a row of 5 in a rows-of-4 order is circled in red). Wrong REFUSAL of a fillable order: a 3-second ghost overlay shows the arrangement that would have worked (e.g., "4 rows of 7 fit the rules") building itself in pale blue in the empty crate, then the captain leaves with the bonus crate ("−10 promised fish"). Wrong REASON on a correct refusal: half credit — the stamp holds, but the harbor master scrawls the true reason over the child's chosen one, and it counts as a flagged entry in the log. Nothing is hidden: every consequence is a visible change in stock, log, and dock.
input.recovery: Recovery is structural, never a lecture. After any wrong stamp, the very next order is a "steady order" — same constraint type, smaller product, generous margin — so the child immediately re-earns footing and a small stock rebate ("+4 fish, dock scraps recovered") for getting it right. Inside any single order, near-misses are free: fish drag back to stock with no penalty, and after 90 seconds of rearranging on one order the wharf cat hops onto the conveyor and paws at whichever constraint badge is being neglected (pure attention direction, no answer given). If stock ever drops below what the remaining shift needs, a "salvage order" appears — a genuinely fillable easy order worth bonus stock — so the shift can always be completed, though the final tally honestly records the rough night.
progression: Orders 1–2 (warm hands): single-constraint fresh items — "pack 12, exactly 3 per row" then "pack 21, exactly 3 rows" (missing factor by building). Both fillable. Teaches the grid, the lock, the SHIP stamp, and the stock cost of sloppiness at low risk.

Order 3 (the door opens): first genuinely impossible single-constraint order — "pack 17 in equal rows of more than one fish." Every arrangement leaves a red stub. First legitimate use of CANNOT BE PACKED plus reason selection ("nothing divides it evenly"). This is the moment refusal is modeled as a real answer.

Orders 4–5 (two rules at once): dual-constraint fillable orders — "pack 24, more than 2 rows AND fewer than 6 fish per row" (4×6 fails a rule, 6×4 works — the salience trap made visible by the gold badges), then "pack 30, an even number of rows AND more than 4 per row."

Order 6 (two rules, no exit): dual-constraint impossible — "pack 25 in exactly 4 equal rows" or "pack 24 with more than 4 rows AND more than 4 per row." The child must exhaust or reason past near-misses and stamp refusal with the right reason ("the rule breaks the count").

Order 7 (the squeeze): the stock-pressure order — a large fillable order (e.g., "pack 28, exactly 4 rows") that is only affordable if earlier stock was protected; if stock is short, the salvage-order path opens first. Makes earlier decisions retroactively meaningful.

Order 8 (final — choose then build): the Festival Team Challenge order. Two candidate crates sit on the dock — e.g., 32 fish and 27 fish — under the rule "equal rows of exactly 8." Only one candidate can obey the rule. The child must first CHOOSE the quantity (committing the other crate back to the boat), then build it correctly. Choosing wrong strands them with an impossible build they must then refuse — recoverable but costly. This is full synthesis: judge two products against constraints before touching a single fish.

Shift end: the harbor master reads the log aloud, and reads the child's REFUSALS proudest of all — "Order 3: refused. Reason: nothing divides seventeen evenly. That's a packer's eye, that is." Tally shown (shipped, refused, spilled, stock remaining). No mastery language; the record is stamped and slid into the harbor log drawer, awaiting the harbor master's morning review.
input.visualDirection: Warm-lantern-against-cold-night palette: deep indigo harbor and rain outside the window; amber lamplight pooling on worn wooden planks inside. Fish are chunky, satisfying silver-blue sprites with a slight wet sheen and squash-and-stretch on pickup. The crate grid is honest carpentry — visible nail heads, rope handles — with locked rows glowing calm ice-blue and illegal rows pulsing warning red with a subtle wobble. Order slips are cream paper with big stamped numerals and two constraint badges that flip grey→gold when satisfied; typography is large, high-contrast, readable by a 9-year-old at a glance. The stock pile is drawn as a literal heap that shrinks in visible chunks. Stamps are oversized rubber stamps with ink texture; the refusal stamp leaves a proud red seal, not a shameful X. Everything readable in one screen, no scrolling, decision surface always visible.
input.engagementPrediction: Prior evidence shows this child rates construction-style, self-paced activities highest (5s with replay on construction and adapted routes) and abandoned the speed-pressure route (2). This design is therefore hands-on building with zero timers — pressure comes from resource scarcity and judgment, not clocks. Predicted engagement: high; the drag-build loop matches their demonstrated construction appetite, the stock economy gives the paced tension they tolerated well, and the refusal stamp offers a novel power move. Predicted friction point: Order 3 (first impossible order) may produce 60–120s of near-miss rearranging before the first refusal, exactly as the Planner prediction anticipates — this is the instrument working, not disengagement, and the free drag-back plus cat nudge keep it from tipping into frustration. Falsification signal: abandonment or three consecutive wrong stamps without rearrangement attempts.
input.audienceRationale: For a 9-year-old, third grade, with fresh unassisted 3/3 transfer evidence on equal groups, missing factor, and word-problem interpretation, and a resolved-looking uniqueness misconception that has never been tested against impossibility. The design speaks in concrete physical language (fish, crates, rows) rather than symbolic notation; every constraint is checkable by eye via badges; reading load is minimal (orders are under 12 words). The night-shift-alone framing grants the grown-up responsibility 9-year-olds crave, and the harbor master praising refusals directly targets the untested construct: making \"no arrangement exists\" feel like competence, not failure. Numbers stay within 12–32, inside grade-3 fact range, so all cognitive budget goes to constraint synthesis and impossibility judgment — the actual boss skill — not fact retrieval.
input.interactionDemonstration: Order 4 walkthrough: slip reads "PACK 24 — MORE THAN 2 ROWS ✚ FEWER THAN 6 PER ROW." Child, following salience, drags fish into rows of 6 (the familiar 4×6). As the fourth row locks, the count badge goes gold (24 ✓) and the rows badge goes gold (4 rows > 2 ✓) — but the per-row badge stays grey with a small "6 is not fewer than 6" tooltip when tapped. SHIP IT remains dim. Child drags a fish out of the top row; the row unlocks and glows red. They tear down to rows of 4: six rows lock one by one — CLUNK, CLUNK — and on the sixth, all three badges flare gold simultaneously, SHIP IT ignites green, the child slams it, the crate lid drops, a nail-gun triple-tap seals it, and the conveyor carries it out into the night as the stock counter holds steady and the log gains a green entry. The math (24 = 6×4 but not 4×6 under these rules) was the entire mechanism of the moment.
input.interactionContinuity: One continuous shift, one continuous interaction grammar. The drag-build-lock-stamp loop established in the first ten seconds never changes; only the orders deepen (one rule → two rules → impossibility → stock squeeze → choose-then-build). The conveyor is the sole scene-transition device — orders slide in, crates slide out — so there are no menus, cutscenes, or mode switches anywhere in the experience. Stock, log, and dock persist visibly across all eight orders, making every decision feel like part of one accumulating night rather than a sequence of disconnected problems. The final choose-then-build order uses the identical grid and stamps; only the judgment demanded has grown.
input.worldReaction: The world answers every mathematical act physically. Correct rows lock with a wooden clunk and ice-blue glow; illegal rows wobble red and refuse. Correct shipments: lid slams, nails fire, the crate rides the conveyor out, a distant boat horn approves, the harbor log gains a green stamped line. Correct refusals: the red seal thuds down, the order slip is spiked on the refusal spike with the chosen reason printed on it, and the harbor master's silhouette at the office window gives a slow nod. Wrong shipments: crane hoist, trapdoor, splash, gulls scatter, stock pile visibly craters. Wrong refusals: the ghost-array builds itself in pale blue as silent proof, and the captain marches off with the bonus crate. The dock itself keeps score — spiked refusals, stacked shipped crates, and floating debris from spills are all persistently visible set dressing that the child's math has authored.
input.payoff: The shift-end scene: lanterns dim, the conveyor stops, and the harbor master walks the dock reading the night's log aloud in a gravelly, warm voice-line style (text with audio sting). Shipments get a nod — but the refusals get the ceremony: each spiked refusal slip is held up to the lantern and read with the child's chosen reason ("Seventeen. Nothing divides it evenly. Correct call."), because refusing an impossible order is what a real packer does. The full tally appears as a stamped ledger page — orders shipped, orders refused, fish spilled, fish remaining — and the page slides into the harbor log drawer with a final stamp: "RECORDED. AWAITING HARBOR MASTER'S MORNING REVIEW." No mastery is certified; the night simply ends with the child's judgment on the record, and the Festival Team Challenge crate (if earned) sits gleaming on the dock for the team.
input.replayVariation: On replay the order generator reshuffles products and constraints from a fresh-item pool (products 12–36; constraint templates: exact rows, exact per-row, inequality on rows, inequality on per-row, parity of rows, dual inequalities), guaranteeing at least two genuinely impossible orders per shift in new positions so refusal timing can't be memorized. The final choose-then-build candidates change (e.g., 30 vs 26 under "equal rows of exactly 5"). Starting stock and salvage thresholds shift slightly to change the economic texture. A returning child also unlocks "foreman mode" flavor: one order per shift arrives with a smudged number the child must infer from a stated rule plus the visible crate size — same construct, higher inference — keeping the same eight-order shape but never the same night twice.
input.motionDirection: Motion is weighty and dockside-mechanical: fish squash on grab and slap-settle into cells; rows lock with a short compression bounce; the conveyor moves with a rhythmic tick-advance rather than smooth glide. The red illegal-row wobble is a small ±2° oscillation — noticeable, never seizure-adjacent. Stamps descend with anticipation (brief hover, then thump with a 4-frame ink splash). The crane-dunk is the biggest animation in the game (hoist, pause, trapdoor, splash, gull scatter) and is reserved exclusively for wrong shipments so its drama carries meaning. Ghost-array builds animate row by row at readable speed (~350ms per row). All motion uses ease-out timing under 400ms except the two ceremony moments (dunk, shift-end reading); nothing animates during the child's active reasoning except the gentle badge glow, keeping the thinking surface calm.
input.soundDirection: Ambient bed: soft rain on the roof, creaking timbers, distant buoy bell, low harbor water lap — loopable, unobtrusive, mixable under thought. Interaction foley: wet slap on fish placement, deep wooden CLUNK on row lock (the game's signature satisfaction sound), papery slide-clack for arriving orders, heavy rubber thud + ink squish for stamps. Success shipment: nail-gun triple-tap, conveyor rumble, distant approving boat horn. Wrong shipment: crane chain rattle, hollow trapdoor bang, big splash, gull cries — dramatic, never a mocking failure jingle. Refusal seal: a proud, resonant thud distinct from the ship stamp, slightly lower in pitch, so refusal sounds authoritative. Shift-end: rain fades, a single warm accordion phrase under the harbor master's reading. No background music during active problem-solving; the sound design lets the child hear their own decisions land.
usefulLibraries: PixiJS (2D WebGL sprite rendering for fish, crate grid, conveyor, water)
GSAP (stamp thumps, crane-dunk sequence, badge flips, ghost-array builds)
Howler.js (layered ambient bed + interaction foley with per-channel volume)
@dnd-kit or interact.js (accessible pointer/touch drag of fish into grid cells)
seedrandom (deterministic per-shift order generation for replay variation and evidence reproducibility)
input.falsifyingEvidence: The design's instrument claims are falsified if: (1) the child ships an uneven/red arrangement path never occurs because the grid blocks it — so instead the falsifiable behavioral signal is stamping CANNOT BE PACKED on fillable orders more than twice without any rearrangement attempts, indicating refusal is being used as an escape hatch rather than a judgment (instrument failure: refusal too cheap); (2) the child solves impossible orders by immediate refusal with correct reasons but ALSO refuses fillable dual-constraint orders at >40% rate, indicating the two-constraint load exceeds capacity and the boss is measuring overload, not synthesis; (3) engagement collapse (abandonment, or >3 minutes idle) at Order 3, indicating impossibility-as-answer was not adequately legitimized by the design; (4) the Planner's prediction (satisfy salient rule first, check second after building) fails to appear even once across dual-constraint orders — which would suggest the badges telegraph the second constraint so strongly that the boss cannot observe the predicted behavior, weakening its diagnostic value. Any of these routes the artifact back for revision rather than to calibration.
